According to the specified coordinate method, take D=(0,0), C=(4,0), A=(0,4), B=(4,4), so M=(2,0). The circle with M as center and radius 2 satisfies (x-2)^2+y^2=4, and after simplification gives x^2+y^2=4x. The circle with A as center and radius 4 satisfies x^2+(y-4)^2=16, and after simplification gives x^2+y^2=8y. The intersection points of the two circles satisfy 4x=8y, therefore x=2y. Substituting into x^2+y^2=8y gives (2y)^2+y^2=8y, that is, 5y^2=8y, so y=0 or y=8/5. y=0 corresponds to the intersection point D, therefore the y-coordinate of P is 8/5, and the x-coordinate is 2y=16/5. Segment AD is on the line x=0, so the distance from P to AD is just the x-coordinate of P, namely 16/5.

method.method_draft: Use a synthetic radical-axis and chord-length route. From the image, note that D and P are the two intersections, so DP is the common chord of the two circles. From the text, AD=4, DM=2, AM=sqrt(4^2+2^2)=2sqrt(5). By the radical-axis/common-chord theorem, DP is perpendicular to AM. Therefore the direction of DP has horizontal-to-vertical ratio 2:1. Let N be the foot from M to line DP; since DP is perpendicular to AM, N lies on AM. In triangle ADM, compute MN as the projection of MD onto MA: MN=(MD^2+MA^2-AD^2)/(2MA)=(4+20-16)/(4sqrt(5))=2/sqrt(5). In the smaller circle centered at M with radius 2, the perpendicular from the center to chord DP bisects the chord, so half the chord is sqrt(2^2-(2/sqrt(5))^2)=4/sqrt(5), hence DP=8/sqrt(5). The horizontal component of DP is DP*(2/sqrt(5))=16/5. Since D lies on AD and AD is vertical, this horizontal component is exactly the distance from P to AD.
